name: Two-step verification changed
description: Confirms that two-step verification was switched on — or off — says what changes at the next sign-in, points at the recovery codes, and explains how to reverse it.

origin.note: Design: shield — no alarm and no table. A state bar under the headline, the deltas as a check list, an anti-phishing pair set side by side, and the recovery codes given a pale band of their own.

subject: {{ product.name }} two-step verification: {{ state_word }}
preheader: What changes at your next sign-in, where the recovery codes are, and how to reverse it.

user.first_name.description: Names the person, so a settings change reads as something that happened to their account rather than an announcement. Omitted cleanly when unknown.

enabled.description: True when the control was switched on, false when it was switched off. Drives the mark and the colour of the state bar; it does not write any copy, so the wording stays yours.

state_word.description: The state in one word, set in bold beside the mark and reused in the subject line. It is the reading that has to survive a greyscale screen, so it can never be implied by colour alone.

state_detail.description: The consequence, continuing the sentence the state word starts. Begin it with a dash so the bar reads as one line.
state_detail.default: — your password on its own will no longer sign you in.

heading_text.description: The headline. Name the control and its new state; a reader scanning a notification list should not have to open the mail to learn which way it went.

body.description: What the change means in practice, before any list of details. Say what is now required and what was left alone.
body.default: Signing in to this account now takes two things: your password, and a code from the authenticator app you just registered. Nothing else about the account has changed.

change_line.description: Who made the change and when, if you record it. Provenance is what lets someone recognise a change they did not make; leave it empty rather than guess.
change_line.example: Changed 24 August 2026, 11:02 UTC from a signed-in session on macOS.

changes_title.description: Heading above the list of deltas. Kept separate because teams word it differently — "What changed", "Summary", "Applied".

changes.description: One entry per setting that actually moved, as `text` with an optional `detail` line under it. Listing only real deltas keeps the mail short enough that people read it.

example.detail: Applies to every sign-in on the web and in the mobile apps.

expectations.description: Two cells set side by side, each `heading` plus `text`: what you will ask for, and what you will never ask for. This is the anti-phishing pair, and it belongs in the one email that teaches someone what a code request looks like. Two items only — three do not fit a 320px screen.

example.heading: We will ask for
example.text: Your password, then the six-digit code your authenticator app is showing.

recovery_text.description: Why the codes matter and where to keep them. Most lockouts after a second factor is enabled are people who never read this paragraph.
recovery_text.default: Ten single-use codes are waiting behind the link below. Print them, or keep them in a password manager — they are the only way back in if the phone is lost.

recovery_url.description: Where the codes can be viewed or regenerated. Omit it if your product shows the codes only once at setup, and the band will state the fact without offering a link.

recovery_label.description: Label for the recovery-codes action — the only filled button in this email, because it is the only thing worth doing today.

undo_text.description: How to reverse the change, including what it will cost them. A security control nobody can find the off switch for is a support ticket.
undo_text.default: You can turn two-step verification off again in security settings. You will need your password and a current code to do it.

settings_url.description: Deep link to the security settings page. Rendered as an underlined link rather than a button so it never competes with the recovery codes.

not_you_text.description: The line for the reader who did not make this change. It sits last and stays plain: if it were styled as an alarm, the ninety-nine people who did make the change would read the whole email as one.
not_you_text.default: If you did not make this change, someone else can reach your account. Change your password straight away and get in touch with us.
